items.content_html:
People of a certain age in Serbia remember Chernobyl as a taste. In the summer of 1986, the strawberries came in as usual, red and ripe, and were eaten under a cloud that had drifted west from Soviet Ukraine. Vesna Goldsworthy made the fruit the title of her 2005 memoir, Chernobyl Strawberries, a coming-of-age story set in Belgrade, the capital of then-socialist Yugoslavia. Forty years on, Serbia is preparing to build a nuclear plant of its own.

For decades the question of nuclear power in Serbia was settled. A 1989 moratorium, passed in the shadow of Chernobyl and the final years of Yugoslavia, banned the construction of nuclear plants. Over time it also drained the country of nuclear expertise and hardened a conviction that nuclear power was both dangerous and unnecessary. In November 2024 the government reopened the file. An amendment to the Law on Energy repealed the ban and set out a phased programme for developing nuclear power. Serbia now says it wants a reactor. Whether it can build one, and whether it should, are separate questions. Public debate about this future trajectory was almost entirely absent. The issue has been treated as a technical matter, not unlike many other key strategic energy and climate-related decisions. 

Why Serbia thinks it needs nuclear

Nuclear has been pushed by industry circles for years. The argument starts with a supply squeeze. Demand for electricity is rising while the plants meant to meet it are old and mostly coal-fired. About two-thirds of the country's electricity generation comes from lignite plants, with hydropower supplying most of the rest and (non-hydro) renewables only a small share. 

Demand for electricity is rising.

Official projections have electricity rising from 26.8 percent to 33.7 percent of final energy consumption by 2040, driven by the projected electrification of heating and transport, by digitisation and by hopes of reindustrialisation. Peak demand could rise sharply by mid-century. 

Environmental effects of this brown coal dependency combined with energy poverty are well documented, not least by the Heinrich Böll Foundation’s work in the field, among them some of the worst air pollution on the continent. Despite commitments made as a member of the Energy Community, Serbia has not committed to decarbonising its energy sector. Until now, it seems. 

The strain is already showing. In 2022, with two units of the Nikola Tesla coal complex out of service and a poor year for hydropower, Serbia had to import more than 3TWh of electricity, around 8 percent of what it used, at a heavy cost to the state. Officials warn that without new capacity the country could face regular winter shortfalls in the near future. Import dependence brings its own risk of volatile prices on regional exchanges. 

There is a second, newer pressure, and it points the other way. Since January 2026 the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) has put a carbon price on imports into the bloc, including electricity. It raises the cost of the power Serbia sells. In the meantime, Serbia has hastily introduced its own carbon tax to avoid the EU’s “indirect taxation”. The effects of these measures remain to be seen.  Serbian electricity is so carbon-intensive that the charge is steep. That gives Belgrade a fresh commercial reason, on top of the environmental one, to want low-carbon power that can run around the clock.

This is the promise of nuclear: steady, low-carbon electricity that does not depend on the weather. This is referred to as "baseload", the minimum, round-the-clock demand that never goes away. For a coal-dependent economy under decarbonisation pressure, the pitch is attractive. It is also the easiest part of the story. 

Serbia Is Still in the Very Early Stages of Implementation 

Serbia is following the roadmap set by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), which its national programme translates into three legally defined phases. Phase one tests whether developing nuclear power is justified at all. It is largely a research exercise: a battery of technical, organisational, legal, economic, financial and staffing studies, meant to establish whether the country has the grounds and the capacity to proceed. Phase two develops the programme proper, and ends when the National Assembly, on the government's proposal, adopts a Strategy for the Peaceful Use of Nuclear Energy. Only phase three involves an actual reactor: the design, construction and operation of a plant, and it would be governed by a separate law passed specifically for the purpose. The Ministry of Mining and Energy runs the first two phases; the third, if it is ever reached, would be a different undertaking altogether.

Serbia is at the very start of phase one. The institutions to carry it out are only now in place. In February 2026 the government set up an inter-ministerial expert working group, and by the summer the country's Nuclear Energy Programme Implementing Organisation (NEPIO) was running. NEPIO is not a single body created by a single act; it combines that working group with an internal unit inside the Ministry of Mining and Energy. Its members are drawn from across the state: the Vinča Institute of Nuclear Sciences, the Nikola Tesla Electrical Engineering Institute, the Serbian Nuclear Society, the regulator SRBATOM, the power and transmission utilities, and several ministries from environment to defence. Regulatory oversight sits with SRBATOM, set up under the country's radiation- and nuclear-safety law.

A working reactor is treated as an option only after 2040.

The government wants to finish phase one by mid-2027 and phases one and two together by 2032, at which point it hopes to choose a technology. A working reactor — the substance of phase three — is treated as an option only after 2040. France's EDF is the front-runner to be selected as the strategic partner. It signed a memorandum of understanding in April 2024 and prepared the early feasibility study; it has now been asked to write several of the phase-one studies, with the rest put out to tender. But Serbia is keeping its options open. It has signed or discussed similar memoranda with China's atomic-energy institute, Russia's Rosatom, South Korea's KHNP as well as Slovenia. None of these is binding. But the range of suitors, from Paris to Moscow and Beijing, points to the political choice behind the technical one.

Which Type of Nuclear Power Will Serbia Choose?

Suppose Serbia gets as far as choosing. It will face a decision the whole industry is now arguing about: the large conventional reactor, or the small modular reactor (SMR).

The conventional reactor is a known quantity. A standard light-water design produces 1,000-1,600MW from a single, custom-built, on-site complex. It has decades of operating data behind it, and a poor record on cost and schedule. Europe's recent flagship projects, Britain's Hinkley Point C, France's Flamanville and America's Vogtle, all ran far over budget and behind time. A modern 1,000MW reactor is now reckoned to cost between €5bn and €20bn, several times the price of a coal plant, and often takes more than a decade to build.

The SMR is the fashionable alternative and the source of much of the current excitement, not least in the European Commission. The demand, mainly in the USA, is driven to a large extent by the need to power new data centres. It reverses the logic of the big build. Instead of one large machine, it uses a series of smaller units, usually under 300MW and often much less, manufactured in a factory as standard modules, shipped to site and assembled, with capacity added as needed. The claimed advantages are lower upfront cost per unit, faster and more predictable construction, flexible siting (on a retired coal site, for instance, so no need for a very specific location) and passive safety systems that rely on gravity and convection rather than pumps.

It is an uncertain bet.

The economics are less flattering than the pitch. On the measure that matters most – capital cost per kilowatt of capacity – SMRs are currently more expensive than large reactors, not cheaper. The IEA treats cost parity as a target to be reached only around 2040, when it projects SMR construction costs falling to roughly $4,500/kW in Europe and America. The SMR case rests on a bet that factory serial production will bring costs down over time, which needs someone to take on the expensive first-mover risk of building enough units to prove it. It is an uncertain bet. So far only Russia and China have grid-connected SMRs operating, and no Western commercial unit is yet running. But the picture is moving quickly. EDF's own study looks at both options, the conventional and the fashionable.

Human Resources, Costs, and Environmental Protection Are Challenges

Whichever reactor Serbia might choose, the same obstacles stand in the way, and several matter more than the choice itself.

Serbia's shortage of nuclear expertise is severe.

The most pressing is human resources. Serbia's shortage of nuclear expertise is severe. The 1989 moratorium did not ban teaching or research, but the effect was similar: specialists emigrated, secondary school and university courses in nuclear engineering closed, and the older generation retired with practically no one trained to replace them. Nuclear physics at the University of Belgrade is taught by physicists trained in other fields, and the electrical-engineering faculty has produced, by one unofficial account, no nuclear engineers in 20 years. This is the one point on which every side agrees, and rebuilding the expertise is thought to take 10 to 20 years, about the same time it would take to build the plant.

The economics are no kinder. Beyond the high capital cost, nuclear's levelised cost of electricity is several times that of new solar or wind, around $140–220 per MWh against well under $80 for utility-scale solar and onshore wind, and the gap has widened as renewables have got cheaper, though raw comparisons understate the cost of the storage and back-up that variable power requires. Decommissioning a plant costs €0.8bn-1.3bn, and a deep geological waste store of the kind Finland has built can cost €3bn and must be monitored for centuries. 

Nuclear's levelised cost of electricity is several times that of new solar or wind.

Private insurers will not cover the full cost of a serious accident, so the state becomes the insurer of last resort; the Fukushima clean-up alone has passed $180bn, most of it public money. Then there is the physical aspect, most of it still unstudied in Serbia. Firstly, no seismic study has been developed specifically for the purpose of analysing nuclear-plant construction in Serbia, even though Serbia sits on a moderately active seismic belt and records small tremors most weeks. Secondly, a traditional reactor needs large amounts of cooling water. The Danube, with an average flow of 5,500-6,000 cubic metres a second, could supply it easily, which is why the plausible sites lie along the river. But cooling brings thermal pollution: water returned 5-10°C warmer, lowering oxygen levels and harming river biodiversity. In addition, climate change pressure on freshwater resources, as demonstrated this year, means that low water levels in major rivers could force reactors to close temporarily during prolonged summer droughts, as witnessed in neighbouring countries this summer. 

The country has no store even for low-level material.

On waste, the country has no store even for low-level material, let alone the high-level spent fuel a reactor would produce, which must be kept isolated for hundreds of thousands of years. And there is the accident risk. Nuclear power is genuinely low-carbon, at 10-15 grams of CO2-equivalent per kilowatt-hour over its life, close to wind. But only if you leave out the accidents. 

Germany's experience cuts both ways. Since closing its last reactors in 2023, Germany has kept the lights on with wind and solar, which together now supply close to half its power, backed by coal, gas and imports, much of the imported power being French nuclear. Anke Weidlich, an energy-systems researcher, argues in her recent interview with Die Zeit that this shows a modern grid does not need new nuclear: the services reactors once provided, such as frequency stability and inertia, can increasingly come from batteries, grid-forming inverters and cross-border links. But the same story is a warning. A country that gives up nuclear without enough clean, firm power to replace it ends up leaning on coal and on its neighbours, which is the position Serbia, largely dependent on brown coal, is trying to get out of.

Weak Rule of Law and Corruption Make Implementation Unlikely

There was hardly any public debate, and this is not a mere procedural objection. It is an essential concern which relates not only to public participation and transparency but also to institutional capacities of the state, not just in terms of expertise but in terms of its capacity to govern in a democratic way. With the weak rule of law and failure to tackle corruption as well as a terrible track record of environmental protection, it is almost unimaginable that the project of this magnitude and complexity could ever be implemented or even assured by existing institutions. The Ministry of Mining and Energy's handling of the EDF study is a case in point: it mistakenly published the preliminary version with the tracked changes still unresolved. 

A reactor tolerates neither error in construction nor incompetence in management.

It is hard, in Serbia, not to think of the Novi Sad railway station canopy that collapsed in November 2024, killing sixteen people. A reconstructed piece of infrastructure built with foreign partners, whose failure, and the evasive institutional response that followed, laid bare the state's inability to manage a project far smaller and simpler than a nuclear plant. That is the uncomfortable backdrop to Serbia's atomic ambitions. A reactor tolerates neither error in construction nor incompetence in management. Before any of it, the country must rebuild a lost profession, find tens of billions of euros, write a legal and regulatory system from scratch, satisfy the IAEA now and Euratom later, and choose whose technology, and whose sphere of influence, it will depend on for the next fifty years. Lifting the ban was the simple part.
items.title: Serbia’s Atomic Bet Analysis After 35 years, a ban is lifted. The government is quietly moving forward with its nuclear ambitions. The political discussion is yet to be had. Damjan Rehm Bogunovic

People of a certain age in Serbia remember Chernobyl as a taste. In the summer of 1986, the strawberries came in as usual, red and ripe, and were eaten under a cloud that had drifted west from Soviet Ukraine. Vesna Goldsworthy made the fruit the title of her 2005 memoir, Chernobyl Strawberries, a coming-of-age story set in Belgrade, the capital of then-socialist Yugoslavia. Forty years on, Serbia is preparing to build a nuclear plant of its own.

For decades the question of nuclear power in Serbia was settled. A 1989 moratorium, passed in the shadow of Chernobyl and the final years of Yugoslavia, banned the construction of nuclear plants. Over time it also drained the country of nuclear expertise and hardened a conviction that nuclear power was both dangerous and unnecessary. In November 2024 the government reopened the file. An amendment to the Law on Energy repealed the ban and set out a phased programme for developing nuclear power. Serbia now says it wants a reactor. Whether it can build one, and whether it should, are separate questions. Public debate about this future trajectory was almost entirely absent. The issue has been treated as a technical matter, not unlike many other key strategic energy and climate-related decisions. 

Why Serbia thinks it needs nuclear

Nuclear has been pushed by industry circles for years. The argument starts with a supply squeeze. Demand for electricity is rising while the plants meant to meet it are old and mostly coal-fired. About two-thirds of the country's electricity generation comes from lignite plants, with hydropower supplying most of the rest and (non-hydro) renewables only a small share. 

Demand for electricity is rising.

Official projections have electricity rising from 26.8 percent to 33.7 percent of final energy consumption by 2040, driven by the projected electrification of heating and transport, by digitisation and by hopes of reindustrialisation. Peak demand could rise sharply by mid-century. 

Environmental effects of this brown coal dependency combined with energy poverty are well documented, not least by the Heinrich Böll Foundation’s work in the field, among them some of the worst air pollution on the continent. Despite commitments made as a member of the Energy Community, Serbia has not committed to decarbonising its energy sector. Until now, it seems. 

The strain is already showing. In 2022, with two units of the Nikola Tesla coal complex out of service and a poor year for hydropower, Serbia had to import more than 3TWh of electricity, around 8 percent of what it used, at a heavy cost to the state. Officials warn that without new capacity the country could face regular winter shortfalls in the near future. Import dependence brings its own risk of volatile prices on regional exchanges. 

There is a second, newer pressure, and it points the other way. Since January 2026 the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) has put a carbon price on imports into the bloc, including electricity. It raises the cost of the power Serbia sells. In the meantime, Serbia has hastily introduced its own carbon tax to avoid the EU’s “indirect taxation”. The effects of these measures remain to be seen.  Serbian electricity is so carbon-intensive that the charge is steep. That gives Belgrade a fresh commercial reason, on top of the environmental one, to want low-carbon power that can run around the clock.

This is the promise of nuclear: steady, low-carbon electricity that does not depend on the weather. This is referred to as "baseload", the minimum, round-the-clock demand that never goes away. For a coal-dependent economy under decarbonisation pressure, the pitch is attractive. It is also the easiest part of the story. 

Serbia Is Still in the Very Early Stages of Implementation 

Serbia is following the roadmap set by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), which its national programme translates into three legally defined phases. Phase one tests whether developing nuclear power is justified at all. It is largely a research exercise: a battery of technical, organisational, legal, economic, financial and staffing studies, meant to establish whether the country has the grounds and the capacity to proceed. Phase two develops the programme proper, and ends when the National Assembly, on the government's proposal, adopts a Strategy for the Peaceful Use of Nuclear Energy. Only phase three involves an actual reactor: the design, construction and operation of a plant, and it would be governed by a separate law passed specifically for the purpose. The Ministry of Mining and Energy runs the first two phases; the third, if it is ever reached, would be a different undertaking altogether.

Serbia is at the very start of phase one. The institutions to carry it out are only now in place. In February 2026 the government set up an inter-ministerial expert working group, and by the summer the country's Nuclear Energy Programme Implementing Organisation (NEPIO) was running. NEPIO is not a single body created by a single act; it combines that working group with an internal unit inside the Ministry of Mining and Energy. Its members are drawn from across the state: the Vinča Institute of Nuclear Sciences, the Nikola Tesla Electrical Engineering Institute, the Serbian Nuclear Society, the regulator SRBATOM, the power and transmission utilities, and several ministries from environment to defence. Regulatory oversight sits with SRBATOM, set up under the country's radiation- and nuclear-safety law.

A working reactor is treated as an option only after 2040.

The government wants to finish phase one by mid-2027 and phases one and two together by 2032, at which point it hopes to choose a technology. A working reactor — the substance of phase three — is treated as an option only after 2040. France's EDF is the front-runner to be selected as the strategic partner. It signed a memorandum of understanding in April 2024 and prepared the early feasibility study; it has now been asked to write several of the phase-one studies, with the rest put out to tender. But Serbia is keeping its options open. It has signed or discussed similar memoranda with China's atomic-energy institute, Russia's Rosatom, South Korea's KHNP as well as Slovenia. None of these is binding. But the range of suitors, from Paris to Moscow and Beijing, points to the political choice behind the technical one.

Which Type of Nuclear Power Will Serbia Choose?

Suppose Serbia gets as far as choosing. It will face a decision the whole industry is now arguing about: the large conventional reactor, or the small modular reactor (SMR).

The conventional reactor is a known quantity. A standard light-water design produces 1,000-1,600MW from a single, custom-built, on-site complex. It has decades of operating data behind it, and a poor record on cost and schedule. Europe's recent flagship projects, Britain's Hinkley Point C, France's Flamanville and America's Vogtle, all ran far over budget and behind time. items.content_html:
The state-organized funeral of Ratko Mladić, commander-in-chief of the Serb forces during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, has rightly drawn public attention in Serbia and internationally. Mladić was a military commander who, at the time of his death, was serving a life sentence imposed on him in 2017 by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia for war crimes and crimes against humanity, as well as for genocide in Srebrenica. The funeral drew attention because of its sheer scale and its de facto state character, which fell short of a fully official form in only a few details. The direct involvement of the Serbian state was most visible in the army's active participation in the memorial events and the burial. A barely concealed state tribute to the deceased was evident in the presence of a number of government ministers, attending "as private individuals." In the spirit of the "symphonia" between altar and state leadership, the funeral service was conducted personally by the head of the Serbian Orthodox Church. The ruling party, which long ago usurped the state and its mechanisms, organized its phalanxes to "spontaneously" greet, from overpasses and along the road, the vehicle carrying Ratko Mladić's body from Belgrade airport. The body had been flown there from the Netherlands on a Government of Serbia aircraft, accompanied by the Minister of Justice.

In this commentary, I will first point to several precedents showing that such conduct by the Serbian government and part of the Serbian public is not unique in Europe, although it does display certain unsettling specificities. I will then consider the broader circumstances that made such an event possible without stronger public resistance. Finally, I will turn to the specifics of the current political context that served as a catalyst for the inappropriate spectacle we have witnessed.

Precedents

Several elements together constitute an event with no substantively comparable precedent in recent history. These are the extent of the participation of the Serbian state and its institutions in the funeral of a person convicted of crimes under international criminal and humanitarian law, the officiating of the highest church leader, and the presence of several thousand citizens. The Archive of Public Gatherings (Arhiv javnih skupova), an organization that monitors public assemblies, estimated attendance at around 16,000. Admittedly, there have been comparable situations, but their "controversiality" falls short of the event discussed here. I do not intend to suggest any equivalence in terms of ideological profiles, the scale of crimes, or any other parallels, since such comparisons always carry a risk of anachronism or relativization in historical accounts. Even so, one dimension is clearly comparable across different contexts: the attitude of the state and the public toward persons convicted of crimes at the moment of their death.

As is well known, the senior Nazi military and civilian officials sentenced to death at Nuremberg were for the most part left without a known grave. By contrast, individuals who served fixed prison terms and completed them were, after their deaths, usually buried within the family circle, with modest funeral rites. One exception, which comes somewhat closer to the funeral of Ratko Mladić, is the funeral of Admiral Karl Dönitz, Hitler's successor at the head of the Third Reich. However, the parallel lies primarily in the event as a public (not state) manifestation and in the presence of several thousand citizens and Dönitz's comrades-in-arms, Wehrmacht veterans. Any involvement of the German state was entirely absent in this case. Moreover, the German authorities of the time explicitly ordered that Dönitz be denied all the military honors that an officer of his rank would otherwise have been entitled to. No active-duty service member was permitted to appear at the funeral in uniform, an order some officers ignored. In short, the funeral of Karl Dönitz, who was convicted after the end of the war, was a relatively large event. It included the appropriate church ritual and an honor guard of veterans holding high military decorations, and it took place under the sign of informally expressed high esteem for the deceased top Nazi official. Yet somewhat earlier, in 1973, one of the field marshals of the Third Reich, Erich von Manstein, had been buried in Germany with military honors; he had been sentenced to a multi-year prison term in 1949. There was a clear difference in the treatment of these two convicted Wehrmacht officers. Although both held high rank, Dönitz's membership in Hitler's innermost circle and in the leadership of the Third Reich was an insurmountable obstacle to granting him official posthumous honors.

A more recent example is the funeral of Croatian general Slobodan Praljak, who was convicted in The Hague. General Praljak's body was transported to Zagreb under special measures and with the utmost discretion. A private farewell at Mirogoj cemetery was held among family and closest friends, in accordance with Praljak's own wishes. However, the main public act of tribute was organized by the Croatian Generals' Assembly (Hrvatski generalski zbor), an association of retired generals, at the Vatroslav Lisinski concert hall in Zagreb. The commemoration was attended by around 2,000 people. Among them, though not in the capacity of official state representatives, were the then Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence, the Minister of Croatian Veterans, and the Deputy Speaker of the Croatian Parliament. Numerous other members of parliament, former senior political officials, and generals also attended, including several prominent figures from Croatia's military and veterans-political establishment. On the same day, a senior church dignitary (a bishop) celebrated a requiem mass, attended by numerous generals, war veterans, and other public figures from Croatian politics. The active military was not involved in the event. Even the participation of a choir made up of active service members was not approved, precisely so that the active military would not be associated with the convicted man.

There have been other comparable examples in the past, especially if one includes figures who remained unconvicted for crimes that can clearly be attributed to them. The circumstances were generally similar: over time, the retributive character of the attitude toward such a figure weakened, and conviction and punishment usually did not extend post mortem, in the form of a secret burial or the scattering of ashes at an unknown location. The exception in this respect is Rudolf Hess, whose remains were first buried at a known location and later relocated so that the burial site would not become a gathering place for neo-Nazis.

As far as Serbia is concerned, a precedent had already been set with the burial of General Nebojša Pavković in the Alley of Distinguished Citizens. That funeral had a somewhat more official character than Mladić's, with the highest military honors and the official presence of state officials, including an envoy of the President of the Republic. With the funerals of Nebojša Pavković and Ratko Mladić, given the way these events were organized, the Serbian authorities and the part of the Serbian public that took part in them have gone further than in any previous comparable case. They did so in terms of state involvement, scale, and above all the publicity given to these events.

The Broader Context

The main political and social precondition for the state's deep involvement in organizing the funerals of convicted military commanders from the 1990s wars in the former Yugoslavia is a persistently encouraged and widespread belief in Serbia. According to this belief, Serbs were the greatest victims of those wars, and all convictions of members of the Serb side are anti-Serb fabrications or tendentious exaggerations. This is the message continuously communicated by every source of public authority: state officials, most of the intellectual public, and the Serbian Orthodox Church. Dissenting voices are not merely drowned out. Everyone who dares to speak on these issues contrary to the privileged view is publicly discredited, accused of anti-Serb activity, and subjected to aggressive propaganda and verbal violence, which occasionally escalates into physical violence. One journalist has even received a death threat.

In such an environment, any meaningful debate that might call into question the "sacred truths" is not only futile but impossible. These truths concern the alleged lack of objectivity, political bias, anti-Serb orientation, and instrumentalization of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia and the International Court of Justice in The Hague. Both judicial institutions established that the crime in Srebrenica constituted genocide, a finding firmly rejected in Serbia by most of the public that holds any view on the matter. Moreover, even the criminal offence of genocide denial has been drafted in Serbian criminal legislation very carefully and deliberately, so as to exclude the possibility of punishing denial of the Srebrenica genocide. The concept of "dealing with the past" has been promoted almost exclusively through the activities of civil society organizations. In Serbia it has produced very limited results, reduced to individual insights and an almost privatized sense of reverence for the victims, without any public articulation.

The attitude toward the Srebrenica genocide is a particularly telling illustration of this atmosphere. Even when it is "acknowledged" that a crime took place, incomparably more condemnation is directed at those who characterize that crime as genocide than at those who committed it or who deny it, even while glorifying those responsible. Individuals and organizations that consistently advocate respect for the judgments of the Hague tribunal are disqualified far more harshly and far more often than the perpetrators of the crime are criticized, whatever the specific legal qualification may be. And one question in particular arises: why is the qualification "crime against humanity," the alternative qualification of the Srebrenica crime, so much more "appealing" to genocide deniers? What would change in their attitude toward the crime if its qualification were different? These questions are, unfortunately, rhetorical.

For decades, the main "argument" in Serbia that the Srebrenica crime was not genocidal in character has been that Bosniak women and children were not killed, or that the ethnic group of Srebrenica Bosniaks was not destroyed as a whole. The argument is meaningless if only because the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide provides that genocide can be committed against part of a protected group, a point on which the courts have given very detailed reasoning. It is sometimes claimed that the Srebrenica crime was an act of retaliation for the killing of the Serb population. This, again, is an argument without any legal relevance: genocide can be committed even as an act of defence, and retaliation hardly merits discussion. In general, the legal reasoning is very little known to the public, while historical and national-emotional content is widely manipulated. This approach presupposes, of course, the complete public discrediting of the relevant international courts. Under such circumstances, legal argumentation is simply irrelevant.

Under such circumstances, and with the exception of Srebrenica, the attitude toward crimes for which Serb forces and their commanders are responsible is characterized primarily by near-total public silence in Serbia. Domestic court verdicts for war crimes are probably the least communicated output of any state body. Cooperation with the Hague tribunal is implicitly understood as an imposed obligation, a kind of international blackmail that Serbia accepted because it had no other choice. This has produced an atmosphere in which every member of the opposing side's armed forces is implicitly a criminal, while every member of the Serb forces is either innocent or all but forced into committing a crime by various turns of circumstance. The usual mantra involves an "objective" confesion that "there were crimes on our side too." However, knowledge of those crimes, or any unequivocal ethical distancing from them, is almost entirely absent, apart from the trite and unconvincing "condemnation of all crimes." How exactly does Serbian society confront these "crimes of ours"? What exactly is the ethical distance being established from, when both the crimes and their perpetrators are at best unknown to the public, while the known ones are excused in every possible way? What real effect does an abstract condemnation of "all crimes" have, without any concreteness that would give the position meaning, awaken empathy with the victims, and take a clear stance on the act itself and its perpetrators?

At the root of this attitude toward the wars and the crimes which were committed lies a perspective whose deep entrenchment is inversely proportional to its ethical and intellectual shallowness. This is the unconditional privileging of national-identity commitments, which are placed above every universal ethical principle. In terms of values and ethics, the national not only precedes every other consideration but becomes the only recognized value, even more so the greater its divergence from other considerations. Few, of course, will openly admit this, but the vast majority live out this lamentable proportion, blissfully convinced of the moral and ethical superiority of their own group. This unquestioned belief  is not relativised in the slightest. On the contrary, it is reinforced by the abstract phrase "there were crimes on our side too." This "generous" phrase serves only one purpose. It strips the prior belief in one's own moral superiority of the implausibility, the absurd unconvincingness, and the almost psychopathic detachment from reality that its absolutization inevitably entails, even from the perspective of the most impartial individual. In reality, however, the cognitive mechanism of this construct functions precisely without any concrete content behind that admission.

None of the above necessarily applies to the majority of society. It is in fact unlikely that most people sincerely participate in such a construction of reality. A model of conformism, combined with consciously chosen or unconsciously adopted indifference, is a far more convincing explanation. The problem for society, however, lies in those moments when circumstances force people to take a position. At such moments, there is no one to effectively oppose the privileged paradigm.

The Specific Context

Serbia's current ruling structures are not merely beneficiaries of the situation described above; they are among its active creators. The ruling clique's media machinery continuously, persistently, daily, and around the clock reproduces content that reinforces ethnocentric and moralizing nationalist attitudes on every socially relevant issue. In this way the ruling structure achieves two goals: the complete marginalization of opposing views, and the sidelining of those actors who claim to represent the same principles more authentically. In this respect, the government and its nationalist alternative are structurally engaged in the same task and share the same views. The specific current context in which Ratko Mladić's funeral should be viewed is largely shaped by their concrete relationship.

Ratko Mladić's funeral should therefore be viewed in light of the context outlined above, with current political circumstances in Serbia acting as a catalyst that further accentuated clearly recognizable tendencies. The ruling political organization is facing its strongest challenge ever from a political grouping built on a catch-all principle, which has managed to win over a large number of right-leaning voters. Until now, the current regime had managed to distribute this segment of the electorate among several obviously "satellite" political groupings that posed as the opposition. items.title: The Funeral of Ratko Mladić: Between Political Rally and Opportunistic Grotesque Commentary Serbia formally bid farewell to Ratko Mladić without a state funeral. Yet the state arranged the transport of his body, the military took part in the ceremony, the head of the Serbian Orthodox Church officiated the service, and ruling-party structures organized “spontaneous” gatherings along the route. The funeral thus became a political event and an opportunity for the authorities to instrumentalize a dead body to send messages to both domestic and international audiences. Srđan Milošević
items.summary:
The state-organized funeral of Ratko Mladić, commander-in-chief of the Serb forces during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, has rightly drawn public attention in Serbia and internationally. Mladić was a military commander who, at the time of his death, was serving a life sentence imposed on him in 2017 by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia for war crimes and crimes against humanity, as well as for genocide in Srebrenica. The funeral drew attention because of its sheer scale and its de facto state character, which fell short of a fully official form in only a few details. The direct involvement of the Serbian state was most visible in the army's active participation in the memorial events and the burial. A barely concealed state tribute to the deceased was evident in the presence of a number of government ministers, attending "as private individuals." In the spirit of the "symphonia" between altar and state leadership, the funeral service was conducted personally by the head of the Serbian Orthodox Church. The ruling party, which long ago usurped the state and its mechanisms, organized its phalanxes to "spontaneously" greet, from overpasses and along the road, the vehicle carrying Ratko Mladić's body from Belgrade airport. The body had been flown there from the Netherlands on a Government of Serbia aircraft, accompanied by the Minister of Justice.

In this commentary, I will first point to several precedents showing that such conduct by the Serbian government and part of the Serbian public is not unique in Europe, although it does display certain unsettling specificities. I will then consider the broader circumstances that made such an event possible without stronger public resistance. Finally, I will turn to the specifics of the current political context that served as a catalyst for the inappropriate spectacle we have witnessed.

Precedents

Several elements together constitute an event with no substantively comparable precedent in recent history. These are the extent of the participation of the Serbian state and its institutions in the funeral of a person convicted of crimes under international criminal and humanitarian law, the officiating of the highest church leader, and the presence of several thousand citizens. The Archive of Public Gatherings (Arhiv javnih skupova), an organization that monitors public assemblies, estimated attendance at around 16,000. Admittedly, there have been comparable situations, but their "controversiality" falls short of the event discussed here. I do not intend to suggest any equivalence in terms of ideological profiles, the scale of crimes, or any other parallels, since such comparisons always carry a risk of anachronism or relativization in historical accounts. Even so, one dimension is clearly comparable across different contexts: the attitude of the state and the public toward persons convicted of crimes at the moment of their death.

As is well known, the senior Nazi military and civilian officials sentenced to death at Nuremberg were for the most part left without a known grave. By contrast, individuals who served fixed prison terms and completed them were, after their deaths, usually buried within the family circle, with modest funeral rites. One exception, which comes somewhat closer to the funeral of Ratko Mladić, is the funeral of Admiral Karl Dönitz, Hitler's successor at the head of the Third Reich. However, the parallel lies primarily in the event as a public (not state) manifestation and in the presence of several thousand citizens and Dönitz's comrades-in-arms, Wehrmacht veterans. Any involvement of the German state was entirely absent in this case. Moreover, the German authorities of the time explicitly ordered that Dönitz be denied all the military honors that an officer of his rank would otherwise have been entitled to. No active-duty service member was permitted to appear at the funeral in uniform, an order some officers ignored. In short, the funeral of Karl Dönitz, who was convicted after the end of the war, was a relatively large event. It included the appropriate church ritual and an honor guard of veterans holding high military decorations, and it took place under the sign of informally expressed high esteem for the deceased top Nazi official. Yet somewhat earlier, in 1973, one of the field marshals of the Third Reich, Erich von Manstein, had been buried in Germany with military honors; he had been sentenced to a multi-year prison term in 1949. There was a clear difference in the treatment of these two convicted Wehrmacht officers. Although both held high rank, Dönitz's membership in Hitler's innermost circle and in the leadership of the Third Reich was an insurmountable obstacle to granting him official posthumous honors.

A more recent example is the funeral of Croatian general Slobodan Praljak, who was convicted in The Hague. General Praljak's body was transported to Zagreb under special measures and with the utmost discretion. A private farewell at Mirogoj cemetery was held among family and closest friends, in accordance with Praljak's own wishes. However, the main public act of tribute was organized by the Croatian Generals' Assembly (Hrvatski generalski zbor), an association of retired generals, at the Vatroslav Lisinski concert hall in Zagreb. The commemoration was attended by around 2,000 people. Among them, though not in the capacity of official state representatives, were the then Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence, the Minister of Croatian Veterans, and the Deputy Speaker of the Croatian Parliament. Numerous other members of parliament, former senior political officials, and generals also attended, including several prominent figures from Croatia's military and veterans-political establishment. On the same day, a senior church dignitary (a bishop) celebrated a requiem mass, attended by numerous generals, war veterans, and other public figures from Croatian politics. The active military was not involved in the event. Even the participation of a choir made up of active service members was not approved, precisely so that the active military would not be associated with the convicted man.

There have been other comparable examples in the past, especially if one includes figures who remained unconvicted for crimes that can clearly be attributed to them. The circumstances were generally similar: over time, the retributive character of the attitude toward such a figure weakened, and conviction and punishment usually did not extend post mortem, in the form of a secret burial or the scattering of ashes at an unknown location. The exception in this respect is Rudolf Hess, whose remains were first buried at a known location and later relocated so that the burial site would not become a gathering place for neo-Nazis.

As far as Serbia is concerned, a precedent had already been set with the burial of General Nebojša Pavković in the Alley of Distinguished Citizens. That funeral had a somewhat more official character than Mladić's, with the highest military honors and the official presence of state officials, including an envoy of the President of the Republic. With the funerals of Nebojša Pavković and Ratko Mladić, given the way these events were organized, the Serbian authorities and the part of the Serbian public that took part in them have gone further than in any previous comparable case. They did so in terms of state involvement, scale, and above all the publicity given to these events.

The Broader Context

The main political and social precondition for the state's deep involvement in organizing the funerals of convicted military commanders from the 1990s wars in the former Yugoslavia is a persistently encouraged and widespread belief in Serbia. According to this belief, Serbs were the greatest victims of those wars, and all convictions of members of the Serb side are anti-Serb fabrications or tendentious exaggerations. This is the message continuously communicated by every source of public authority: state officials, most of the intellectual public, and the Serbian Orthodox Church. Dissenting voices are not merely drowned out. Everyone who dares to speak on these issues contrary to the privileged view is publicly discredited, accused of anti-Serb activity, and subjected to aggressive propaganda and verbal violence, which occasionally escalates into physical violence. One journalist has even received a death threat.

In such an environment, any meaningful debate that might call into question the "sacred truths" is not only futile but impossible. These truths concern the alleged lack of objectivity, political bias, anti-Serb orientation, and instrumentalization of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia and the International Court of Justice in The Hague. Both judicial institutions established that the crime in Srebrenica constituted genocide, a finding firmly rejected in Serbia by most of the public that holds any view on the matter. Moreover, even the criminal offence of genocide denial has been drafted in Serbian criminal legislation very carefully and deliberately, so as to exclude the possibility of punishing denial of the Srebrenica genocide. The concept of "dealing with the past" has been promoted almost exclusively through the activities of civil society organizations. In Serbia it has produced very limited results, reduced to individual insights and an almost privatized sense of reverence for the victims, without any public articulation.

The attitude toward the Srebrenica genocide is a particularly telling illustration of this atmosphere. Even when it is "acknowledged" that a crime took place, incomparably more condemnation is directed at those who characterize that crime as genocide than at those who committed it or who deny it, even while glorifying those responsible. Individuals and organizations that consistently advocate respect for the judgments of the Hague tribunal are disqualified far more harshly and far more often than the perpetrators of the crime are criticized, whatever the specific legal qualification may be. And one question in particular arises: why is the qualification "crime against humanity," the alternative qualification of the Srebrenica crime, so much more "appealing" to genocide deniers? What would change in their attitude toward the crime if its qualification were different? These questions are, unfortunately, rhetorical.

For decades, the main "argument" in Serbia that the Srebrenica crime was not genocidal in character has been that Bosniak women and children were not killed, or that the ethnic group of Srebrenica Bosniaks was not destroyed as a whole. The argument is meaningless if only because the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide provides that genocide can be committed against part of a protected group, a point on which the courts have given very detailed reasoning. It is sometimes claimed that the Srebrenica crime was an act of retaliation for the killing of the Serb population. This, again, is an argument without any legal relevance: genocide can be committed even as an act of defence, and retaliation hardly merits discussion. In general, the legal reasoning is very little known to the public, while historical and national-emotional content is widely manipulated. This approach presupposes, of course, the complete public discrediting of the relevant international courts. Under such circumstances, legal argumentation is simply irrelevant.

Under such circumstances, and with the exception of Srebrenica, the attitude toward crimes for which Serb forces and their commanders are responsible is characterized primarily by near-total public silence in Serbia. Domestic court verdicts for war crimes are probably the least communicated output of any state body. Cooperation with the Hague tribunal is implicitly understood as an imposed obligation, a kind of international blackmail that Serbia accepted because it had no other choice. This has produced an atmosphere in which every member of the opposing side's armed forces is implicitly a criminal, while every member of the Serb forces is either innocent or all but forced into committing a crime by various turns of circumstance. The usual mantra involves an "objective" confesion that "there were crimes on our side too." However, knowledge of those crimes, or any unequivocal ethical distancing from them, is almost entirely absent, apart from the trite and unconvincing "condemnation of all crimes." How exactly does Serbian society confront these "crimes of ours"? What exactly is the ethical distance being established from, when both the crimes and their perpetrators are at best unknown to the public, while the known ones are excused in every possible way? What real effect does an abstract condemnation of "all crimes" have, without any concreteness that would give the position meaning, awaken empathy with the victims, and take a clear stance on the act itself and its perpetrators?

At the root of this attitude toward the wars and the crimes which were committed lies a perspective whose deep entrenchment is inversely proportional to its ethical and intellectual shallowness. This is the unconditional privileging of national-identity commitments, which are placed above every universal ethical principle. In terms of values and ethics, the national not only precedes every other consideration but becomes the only recognized value, even more so the greater its divergence from other considerations. Few, of course, will openly admit this, but the vast majority live out this lamentable proportion, blissfully convinced of the moral and ethical superiority of their own group. This unquestioned belief  is not relativised in the slightest. On the contrary, it is reinforced by the abstract phrase "there were crimes on our side too." This "generous" phrase serves only one purpose. It strips the prior belief in one's own moral superiority of the implausibility, the absurd unconvincingness, and the almost psychopathic detachment from reality that its absolutization inevitably entails, even from the perspective of the most impartial individual. In reality, however, the cognitive mechanism of this construct functions precisely without any concrete content behind that admission.

None of the above necessarily applies to the majority of society. It is in fact unlikely that most people sincerely participate in such a construction of reality. A model of conformism, combined with consciously chosen or unconsciously adopted indifference, is a far more convincing explanation. The problem for society, however, lies in those moments when circumstances force people to take a position. At such moments, there is no one to effectively oppose the privileged paradigm.

The Specific Context

items.content_html:
On Sunday 4 October, around 156 million Brazilians will elect a new head of state. Citizens will not only be deciding on the offices of president and vice-president: they will also be electing 27 governors and their deputies, the entire Chamber of Deputies, two-thirds of the Senate, and the members of the state legislatures. The presidential run-off will take place on 25 October. 

A total of twelve candidates are standing for the presidency. However, the decision will be made in the second round between the incumbent President Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro. These two politicians epitomise the deep divides that not only split Brazil but also characterise the whole of Latin America: the far-right and pro-American camp versus the social-democratic camp with its focus on the Global South. Although polls show that the majority of the Brazilian population wants an end to polarisation, it has not been possible to put forward a moderate conservative alternative.

Which Issues Are Dominating the Election Campaign?

Internal security and the fight against crime are at the heart of the debates. Voters are also concerned about future relations with the US and differing interpretations of patriotism.  Furthermore, a complex corruption crisis at the Supreme Federal Court (STF) is casting a shadow over the election campaign. The allegations also target Alexandre de Moraes – the very judge who is regarded as a symbol of democratic resilience and who put the masterminds behind the attempted coup of 8 January 2023 behind bars. This could also cost Lula crucial percentage points. 

Economic issues, by contrast, are playing hardly any role. Whilst the Brazilian economy is producing solid figures, the current government has failed to capitalise politically on these successes.

What Might Potentially Change in the Coming Parliamentary Term?

Lula da Silva’s advanced age (80) highlights how urgently the Brazilian left needs to modernise and usher in a generational change. The country therefore faces a truly pivotal election in 2030. Until then, the current crisis of confidence in the Supreme Federal Court (STF) threatens a key pillar of democracy, whilst the countless contradictions and the lack of fundamental debates are weakening the Workers’ Party (PT) from within.

Within federal politics, policy shifts are likely to be less significant than hoped for. The composition of Congress is unlikely to change much. The divisions run along familiar lines of conflict: unchecked versus controlled exploitation of natural resources; radical versus gradual disenfranchisement of Indigenous peoples and Quilombolas (descendants of escaped enslaved people), particularly in relation to mining projects with global implications; intensified versus reduced discrimination against minorities and poorer sections of the population; and the dismantling of social policy versus attempts to further strengthen the rule of law.

Significantly more noticeable changes are to be expected in foreign policy. Here, different approaches clash: a self-assured foreign policy versus a more submissive one. On the one hand, the aim is to play an active role in shaping the policies of the Global South in forums such as the G20, BRICS and UN Climate Conferences (COPs). On the other hand, there is a risk of subordination to US claims of hegemony in Latin America – for example, within the framework of the US security initiative ‘Shields of the Americas’. As a result, Brazil might fall silent on the regional and global stage.

The victory of a far-right federal government threatens to put civil society and progressive forces under immense pressure. An existing ‘agents’ law’ – similar to legislation in other countries in the region – could be implemented swiftly. This would cut off foreign funding and restrict the scope for action of progressive actors. Only time will tell to what extent global networks of democratic actors can mitigate this development.

What Does This Mean for Brazil, the Region and Europe?

In Brazil, entrenched power structures continue to shape developments. Interest-driven networks block genuine change. To illustrate: around 20 per cent of the national budget flows directly through MPs and senators to their constituencies, serving clientelist interests. This mechanism is controlled by the so-called Centrão – a conservative coalition of around eight parties with shifting alliances, in which agribusiness is strongly represented. The crucial question is: how much longer will this Centrão coalition be able to withstand the pressure from the far right and the encroaching organised crime? 

There is a great deal at stake, both regionally and globally. Brazil is one of the last countries in the region not to be governed by a right-wing government. A victory for Flávio Bolsonaro would completely shift the balance of power: the region would come under US influence almost in its entirety. This would see the Monroe Doctrine implemented in a new form (Donroe) and the ‘Shield of the Americas’ security alliance activated. In terms of foreign policy, Latin America would lose its voice in global forums such as BRICS or the G20. Instead, authoritarian governments would dominate the scene. For the European Union, a change in power would have serious consequences: it would lose an important partner on key issues such as trade and climate policy, as well as on initiatives to reshape the global order.

This Election Is Also About Addressing the Inequality Gap

Much of the debate is also reminiscent of Germany – above all the call for a strong, stable centre. To counter the Lula-Bolsonaro polarisation in the near future, democratic political forces must reposition themselves, together with civil society. Members of both houses of Congress also have a role to play. They wield enormous power and must fulfil their legislative responsibilities in order to safeguard the balance of power within the state. Why is this so difficult?

At its core, this election is also about addressing the inequality gap: the top one per cent of the population earns ten times as much as the average; estates of over 1,000 hectares continue to account for 45 per cent of the total agricultural land – and it is precisely these large landowners who make up over 80 per cent of the members of Congress (449 out of 513). 

These figures illustrate how far we still have to go to achieve genuine representation of the ‘political centre’, if by that we mean the centre and the majority of society. Lula da Silva stands for the fight against poverty and hunger and thus aims to pursue policies for broad sections of the population who, however, have hardly any voice in Congress. This closes the vicious circle of Brazilian democracy: a parliamentary majority that governs without regard for the interests of a large part of the population.
items.title: Brazil Votes: Where Is the Divided Country Heading? Analysis On 4 October, Brazil will elect a new head of state. Our office director Regine Schönenberg analyses what is at stake globally and why neither Lula da Silva nor Flávio Bolsonaro would change the country’s entrenched power dynamics. Regine Schönenberg

There is a great deal at stake, both regionally and globally. Brazil is one of the last countries in the region not to be governed by a right-wing government. A victory for Flávio Bolsonaro would completely shift the balance of power: the region would come under US influence almost in its entirety. This would see the Monroe Doctrine implemented in a new form (Donroe) and the ‘Shield of the Americas’ security alliance activated. In terms of foreign policy, Latin America would lose its voice in global forums such as BRICS or the G20. Instead, authoritarian governments would dominate the scene. For the European Union, a change in power would have serious consequences: it would lose an important partner on key issues such as trade and climate policy, as well as on initiatives to reshape the global order.

This Election Is Also About Addressing the Inequality Gap

Much of the debate is also reminiscent of Germany – above all the call for a strong, stable centre. To counter the Lula-Bolsonaro polarisation in the near future, democratic political forces must reposition themselves, together with civil society. Members of both houses of Congress also have a role to play. They wield enormous power and must fulfil their legislative responsibilities in order to safeguard the balance of power within the state. Why is this so difficult?

At its core, this election is also about addressing the inequality gap: the top one per cent of the population earns ten times as much as the average; estates of over 1,000 hectares continue to account for 45 per cent of the total agricultural land – and it is precisely these large landowners who make up over 80 per cent of the members of Congress (449 out of 513). 

These figures illustrate how far we still have to go to achieve genuine representation of the ‘political centre’, if by that we mean the centre and the majority of society. Lula da Silva stands for the fight against poverty and hunger and thus aims to pursue policies for broad sections of the population who, however, have hardly any voice in Congress. This closes the vicious circle of Brazilian democracy: a parliamentary majority that governs without regard for the interests of a large part of the population.

At the heart of Tirana, 38 remarkable and threatened species have taken monumental form. Presented on Skanderbeg Square, the new glass mosaic of the Albania Is Biodiversity campaign makes visible something Europe has yet to fully recognise: Albania is one of the continent’s great ecological treasures.

Biodiversity sustains the natural systems on which all life depends. Plants, animals and microorganisms keep ecosystems functioning, secure our food supply and provide clean air and water. Biodiversity is not a luxury. It is the foundation of our existence.

Yet European nature is in deep crisis. According to the European Environment Agency, 81 per cent of habitats assessed under EU nature legislation are in poor or bad conservation status. Wetlands, dunes and coastal ecosystems are under particular pressure. Intensive land use, urbanisation, infrastructure development, pollution and climate change are fragmenting ecosystems and accelerating the loss of species and habitats.

Across much of Europe, this damage has accumulated over generations, leaving natural habitats smaller, more isolated and less resilient. However, this is not the whole European story. The Balkans still contain landscapes of a scale, continuity and diversity that have become rare elsewhere. We therefore need a new narrative for this region. The Balkans are not merely Europe’s periphery. They preserve something that Europe increasingly lacks and needs for its future.

This is precisely why Albania matters

Albania covers only 28,748 square kilometres, less than 0.3 per cent of Europe’s surface area. Yet it contains an extraordinary concentration of plant and animal life. More than 350 bird species have been recorded here. The country provides habitats for emblematic and endangered species ranging from the Balkan lynx and Egyptian vulture to the Dalmatian pelican and Mediterranean monk seal. Albania is an ecological powerhouse for Europe.

The country owes this richness to the remarkable variety of its landscapes and climate zones. Mediterranean and Central European influences overlap. Mountains rise steeply from the Adriatic and Ionian coasts. Free-flowing rivers, ancient forests, alpine meadows, lakes, wetlands and lagoons form a connected mosaic of life.

Albania also lies on the Adriatic Flyway, a key migration route between northern Europe and Africa. Migratory birds depend on its wetlands and lagoons to rest and feed during their long journeys. These places form part of an ecological network that extends far beyond national borders.

Yet Albania’s natural wealth is by no means secure in the long term. Speculative real estate investment, tourism development insufficiently guided by environmental considerations, the increasingly intensive use of natural areas and climate change are placing its coasts, rivers, wetlands and mountain landscapes under growing pressure. Albania still has the opportunity to preserve what, across much of Europe, can now be recovered only through complex and costly ecological restoration.

Together with PPNEA, Albania’s oldest nature conservation organisation and BirdLife International’s Partner in the country, we launched Albania Is Biodiversity in 2023. The campaign stands for a new way of understanding Albania and the Balkans.

For the campaign, artist Kleidi Eski brought Albania’s remarkable and threatened species together in a reinterpretation of the iconic mosaic on the façade of Tirana’s National Historical Museum. The image first appeared in 2023 as a temporary intervention on Skanderbeg Square. It has now been transformed into a monumental glass mosaic.


Hundreds of thousands of individual pieces come together to create a single image of interdependence. Like an ecosystem, the work draws its strength from the interplay of different elements. It invites us to see Albania and the Balkans with new eyes.

European integration cannot simply mean that candidate countries adapt to Europe. Europe must also recognise what these countries contribute to our shared future. Albania brings free-flowing rivers, ancient forests, coastal wetlands, local knowledge and extraordinary biodiversity. These values belong at the heart of European integration. Europe will prove the credibility of its green and democratic promises not only in its current member states, but in how it recognises and protects the natural commons of future members.

The accession process offers practical means to translate this principle into policy. European environmental standards should apply throughout that process. The cumulative effects of infrastructure and tourism investments on ecosystems must be carefully assessed. Independent local conservation organisations need reliable support, and intact habitats should be protected before their loss makes costly restoration necessary.

Implementing this agenda requires lasting partnerships, strong and accountable institutions, scientific cooperation and regional policies that combine economic opportunity with the protection of nature. It also means ensuring that the communities and organisations caring for these landscapes have a voice in the decisions shaping their future.

Albania is not simply on its way to Europe. Ecologically, it has always been at its heart. Albania Is Biodiversity. And Albania’s biodiversity is a European responsibility.

This article first appeared here: al.boell.org
items.title: Albania Is Biodiversity: What Europe Must Recognise and Protect Backgrounder Albania’s extraordinary biodiversity is a shared European asset. Europe must recognise its value, understand it as part of our common future and act decisively to protect it. Dr. Mehmet Gökhan Tuncer

items.content_html:
For years, Germany’s wind energy success story has been the subject of worldwide admiration. Delegations from elsewhere in Europe, US states, and numerous emerging economies came to see for themselves, leaving inspired by our approach. Yet instead of looking back with pride and pressing ahead with determination, we were stricken by the fear of success and slowed the pace of development, continuing to rely on gas and oil from Russia as supposedly cheap energy sources. China seized this opportunity to copy the German model and become the market leader in wind technology. Thousands of jobs in our domestic wind industry were lost. Today, the gravity of this error is becoming clear.

With Russia’s war on Ukraine and the Zeitenwende, including in relation to dependence on Russian energy, the consequences of decelerating the energy transition have come back to haunt us. Had Germany pursued its path with more alacrity and consistency, industry and consumers would not have been so hard hit by the ever-rising energy prices caused primarily by a distorted energy import market. Added to this are high tax burdens, which have made the conversion of wind power into stored energy, hydrogen, or synthetic, emission-free fuels uneconomical. But it is by no means too late to turn this situation around. In just a few years, we can establish a totally new basis for our economy.
I recall the year 2020, when, as a member of the Schleswig-Holstein state government and after a long struggle, I was able to secure the designation of two per cent of the state’s land area as priority zones for wind energy. This laid the foundation that enabled Tobias Goldschmidt, my successor as minister for the energy transition, to announce in August this year that the target of 10 gigawatts of onshore wind energy generation capacity had been achieved. This alone represents half of the output of the entire nuclear power sector in Germany at its peak. Wind energy is now the most important source of electricity in Germany. Twenty years ago, this would have been unthinkable.

While the myth of the “expensive energy transition” is currently being peddled, this could not be further from the truth. According to surveys by the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems (ISE), wind energy – at five to 10 cents per kilowatt-hour – is by far the cheapest form of electricity generation after ground-mounted photovoltaics. Even modern gas-fired power stations incur costs that are almost twice as high, not to mention the production costs of nuclear power, which are many times higher, without even taking into account increasing shortfalls in output due to climate-related shutdowns. The truth is that wind energy is our strongest safeguard against the “hidden” cost drivers that are increasingly becoming visible.

While wind energy has the potential to create jobs and generate added value in many parts of Germany and Europe more broadly, in addition to guaranteeing an affordable supply of electricity, our dependence on conventional energy sources poses an ever-growing threat to security and prosperity. The war in Iran, with the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, has brought home once again how vulnerable we are to supply bottlenecks and price fluctuations. What’s more, the consumption of gas and oil on the world market inevitably leads to additional income for Putin’s Russia, which still exports large quantities of these commodities as well as a significant proportion of the world’s uranium, allowing it to finance what is now the fifth year of its war against Ukraine.

As the scorching summer of 2026 draws to a close, the immense economic burden caused by rapidly advancing climate change is also becoming apparent. The economy recorded losses of hundreds of millions of euros in June and July alone, not to speak of massive healthcare costs and the many heat-related deaths, which defy quantification and are, above all, a terrible human loss. The scale of municipal investment required for heat resilience measures is becoming clear. Alongside defence, infrastructure renewal, and industrial transformation, this represents the next major strain on public finances. It has become abundantly clear that Germany’s most important source of electricity – wind power – is its most effective safeguard against these ever-rising costs and represents a huge opportunity for Germany and Europe to place their industrial and technological base on a solid footing for the long term.

This text was translated by Katy Nicholson.
